articles.headline: A Dakota Cattle Round-up.
articles.text:
Mr. James Vance, a ranchman, who served his apprenticeship as cowboy and "rounder-up," was yesterday corralled and induced to deliver up some interesting matter about round-ups.

"The round-up is the great event of the stockman's year. It's his Fourth of July, and generally lasts a month and a half. The territorial paper publishes such a notice as this," said Mr. Vance, taking a slip of paper from his wallet: "Round-up No. 5,—Laramie Plains Round-up will meet at the Lower Bridge, near McGillis ranch, on the big Laramie river on June 1, and proceed to work the country between the river and the Black Hills Divide as far south as Red Buttes; from thence it will work in two divisions as far south as Twin Mountains; thence back to Diamond Peak, working up Boulder and intermediate creeks up to the source of the Big Laramie river."

"That," proceeded the gentleman, "is an official announcement to all the stockmen, and they combine and join in together. The ranges are generally about ten miles in extent, though some of them are thirty."

"What's a round-up party?"

"That's an expression we have, and means about ten wagons and as many cowboys, a cook going with each wagon, and every cowboy has a string of about six or ten ponies. The 'out' comes off at 3 o'clock in the morning, under the charge of an experienced foreman. Everybody is on horseback, and the foreman operates something in this manner: He sends one party out on the divide as out pickets, and other parties along the canons and gulches with orders to drive the cattle up to the round-up center—a point previously agreed upon."

"The boys will be gone several days?"

"Oh, no. A good cowboy will ride from thirty to forty miles in the morning, coming up to his pony herd and taking out another one of his ponies just as he needs them. Sometimes a cowboy will ride down three or four ponies in a day. When the foreman 'covers his dog,' as it's called, the cattle are gathered on the prairie in small herds, and then comes the fun. On the wiry, little, fleet-footed Indians ponies, who'll dodge and back, and stop in a twinkling, the cowboy rush into the herds, and shouting, yelling, and swearing, separate the herds, and drive out those having the different owners."

"Then every man has his own brand?"

"Most assuredly. There are no two brands alike. Some are slits, some letters, some holes, and some figures. In fact, there is every conceivable form of mark. When a man wants a brand, he gets it up and has it recorded in the office of the county clerk, in a book that is especially kept for the purpose. All the cowboys are not engaged in 'cutting-out'—that is, getting the cattle that have the same brand all together. Others are busy in holding the herd to prevent a stampede. Thus all the heard are picked out."

"What's done with those that are left?"

"Those where the owner is not known are called estrays, and calves that are away from their mothers are called 'mavericks.'"

"What do you do with these?"

"These mavericks are branded with the mark belonging to the largest female herd in the neighborhood."

"Always at the wind-up of the round-up. The cattle are all driven into a corral, where a fire is burning and the branding irons heated. A cowboy rides in and swinging a lariat over the head of a calf or around his hind legs, secures the hand end of the lariat to his saddle pummel. The calf is quickly thrown, and lies wallowing on the ground. The brand is either burned into his side, or his shoulder or rump, or perhaps the ear is slit, and its done in a second, quicker than I'm telling you. There's a great noise made, but very little confusion. They have the business now systematized so that everything goes like clockwork.—[Cincinnati Sun.
articles.summary: Reprint (Cincinnati Sun) of an interview with ranchman James Vance describing a round-up, its organization, cutting-out, mavericks and branding; the notice he quotes is for the Laramie Plains round-up.

articles.headline: It Won't Work With Cowboys.
articles.text: A confidence chap picked up a New Mexico cowboy on the depot platform a day or two since, and after a chat of a few seconds decided he had struck something soft, and proceeded to work the claim. In a few minutes the sum of ten dollars had been transferred from the cow-puncher's pocket to that of the confidence chap. Just as the transfer was completed, the cowboy noticed the railway policeman approaching, drew his "45," and putting it uncomfortably close to the confidence chap's ear, yelled, "You d—d thief, hand back my twenty-five dollars!" The officer seconded the motion, and although the confidence chap insisted that he only received ten dollars the speaker decided the point against him, and he gave up the amount and disappeared as soon as the caucus adjourned. We don't think that sharp gentlemen will care to tackle one of our prairie dudes again.—[Deming Tribune.
articles.summary: Reprint (Deming Tribune): a New Mexico cowboy, swindled of $10 by a confidence man at a depot, recovers $25 at gunpoint with a railway policeman's help.

articles.text:
The above reward will be paid for information leading to the arrest of any person or persons setting fire to the grass in the cattle sections of Western Dakota.

N. P. Ref. Car Co.
Continental Cattle Co.
Hughes & Simpson.
Dorr Clark.
Clark & Plum.
Dickey Bros.
E. G. Paddock.
articles.summary: Seven cattle concerns offer $250 for information leading to the arrest of anyone setting grass fires in the cattle sections of Western Dakota.

articles.headline: $50 Reward.
articles.text:
The above reward will be paid for the return of the following stock or a proportionate reward will be paid for the return of any of them. The stock consists of the following horses:

One bay mare, one brown mare and one roan mare, all young and branded double or reverse P on left shoulder as advertised in our brand columns. Also one light sorrel pony, white legs and face and branded NC on left shoulder and triangle JP on right shoulder also as advertised in our brand columns.

Gregor Lang,
Medora, Dak.
articles.summary: Gregor Lang of Medora offers $50 for the return of three mares branded with a double or reverse P and a sorrel pony branded NC and triangle JP.

articles.headline: $125 Reward.
articles.text:
The above reward will be paid for the return of the team of large gray horses, half Norman breed, weighing twelve and thirteen hundred pounds, stolen from Belfield, Billings Co., Dak., May 26. No brand on them when stolen.

A. Anderson,
Belfield, Dak.
articles.summary: A. Anderson of Belfield offers $125 for a team of large gray half-Norman horses stolen at Belfield on May 26.

articles.headline: Stockmen's Meeting.
articles.text: There will be a meetidg of Bad Lands stockmen at Medora on Tuesday, September 9, 1884, for the purpose of effecting a permanent organization and making the necessary preparations for the fall round-up. A captain for the round-up will also be selected. Let every stockman be present.
articles.summary: Call for a meeting of Bad Lands stockmen at Medora on Tuesday, September 9, 1884, to form a permanent organization, prepare for the fall round-up and choose a round-up captain.

articles.text: It is estimated that there are now in Montana, including calves, upward of a million cattle, besides horses and sheep.
articles.summary: Montana estimated to hold upward of a million cattle besides horses and sheep.

articles.text: The Swan cattle company of Wyoming are now in the midst of their beef harvest. The company is reported to have 10,000 head of four-year-old steers.
articles.summary: The Swan cattle company of Wyoming is in its beef harvest with 10,000 four-year-old steers.

articles.text: Northern New Mexico cattlemen will make a test case of the sheep protection law and will carry it to the highest court if necessary.—[N. M. Stock Grower.
articles.summary: Clipping (N. M. Stock Grower): northern New Mexico cattlemen to test the sheep protection law.

articles.text: Driscoll & Son last week shipped from Dickinson fifty-eight carloads of fat cattle to Chicago. Their shipments from there this season will amount to about 12,000 head.
articles.summary: Driscoll & Son shipped fifty-eight carloads of fat cattle from Dickinson to Chicago last week; season shipments to reach about 12,000 head.

articles.text: Last Friday two stock trains collided at Columbia, Penn., and a dispatch from Lancaster says the wreck took fire and 800 sheep and hogs were comsumed, only 50 being saved.
articles.summary: Two stock trains collided at Columbia, Penn.; the wreck burned and 800 sheep and hogs died.

articles.text: Texas "bronchos" are being introduced in Asia. A short time ago a train of sixteen cars of Texas horses, mares and stallions, left New Orleans, the destination of which was Constantinople.
articles.summary: Texas horses shipped from New Orleans to Constantinople.

articles.text: Col. Gile, of Ellsworth county, Kansas, says she has thirty-six head of half-breed Short-horn cattle, the product of one cow within the last twelve years besides 20 head sold or slaughtered.—[Kan. L. S. Indicator.
articles.summary: Clipping (Kan. L. S. Indicator): Col. Gile of Ellsworth county, Kansas, on the progeny of one Short-horn cow.

articles.text: The Arab compels his horse to feed from the ground, in order to maintain the curve of the backbone. Come to think of it this is the natural way of feeding, and is an agrument for low mangers.—[N. M. Stock Grower.
articles.summary: Clipping (N. M. Stock Grower) on the Arab practice of feeding horses from the ground.

articles.text: Four carloads of unbroken Colorado bred horses will in a few days be shipped to Europe. They are all half-breed Normans, of good size and style, and will be landed in London and placed upon the market.—[Col. L. S. Record.
articles.summary: Clipping (Col. L. S. Record): four carloads of Colorado half-Norman horses to be shipped to London.

articles.text: The cattle shipments from here this season have already amounted to 295 carloads, or 6,000 head, and it is stated by the railroad officials that a great many more carloads will be shipped before the season is over.—[Dickinson Press.
articles.summary: Clipping (Dickinson Press): cattle shipments from Dickinson this season have reached 295 carloads, or 6,000 head.

articles.text: A gentleman who held the watch on the boys tells us that John Farington and his outfit, at the Quistaque ranch, lately branded 400 calves in just 100 minutes, which is tolerably quick work.—[Mobeetie, (Tex.) Panhandle.
articles.summary: Clipping (Mobeetie Panhandle): John Farington's outfit at the Quistaque ranch branded 400 calves in 100 minutes.

articles.text: For five years I have had a horse with hoofs shelly and brittle, so that it was difficult to keep shoes on him during the dry weather of July and August. In may last I dressed his feet with pine tar, and now repeat it every week, and the hoofs are perfectly sound even in mid-summer.—[H. W. Dunning in the N. Y. Tribune.
articles.summary: Clipping (H. W. Dunning, N. Y. Tribune) on treating brittle hoofs with pine tar.

articles.text: Young men of England have been advised to come to America to engage in raising mutton for the English market. It is predicted that the supply cannot keep pace with the demand. Perhaps the young men of America will do well to consider such advice as being worthy their attention.—[Exchange.
articles.summary: Exchange item advising young Englishmen to raise mutton in America for the English market.

articles.text: If the cattle owners carry out their resolution made early in the season, every bull will be removed from the range in northern Colorado by the first of November. Had this been done last year, two or three hundred thousand dollars would have been saved in the death looses, and the bulls, after being fed through the winter, would have been worth one-third more in the spring.—[Denver (Col.) L. S. Record.
articles.summary: Clipping (Denver L. S. Record): northern Colorado cattle owners resolve to remove bulls from the range by November 1.

articles.text: A man named Brown, one of the trail hands with a Texas herd, was shot and killed on the head of the Frenchman a few days ago by a fellow-herder. The man rode up to the wagon and found Brown asleep under it, went up to him and took his six-shooter, then woke him up and shot him; he then mounted a horse and skipped. The cause was an old grudge. Brown was buried where he was killed.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.
articles.summary: Clipping (N. W. L. S. Journal): trail hand Brown shot and killed by a fellow-herder at the head of the Frenchman.

articles.text: The Ute Indians continue their depredations in Utah and Colorado. They are making times very troublesome for the settlers and stockmen there. The latter had quite a skirmish with them on the Dolores a few days since, in which one Indian and a number of horses on both sides were killed. Cattle are being gathered with cavalry escort and a serious outbreak from the Utes and Navajos is expected to occur at any time.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.
articles.summary: Clipping (N. W. L. S. Journal): Ute depredations in Utah and Colorado and a skirmish on the Dolores.

articles.text: The Cherokee nation think of holding a convention soon, to consider the wire fence monopoly of the land and kindred questions. It is sad to see the dying struggles of the Indian, in his foolish endeavor to keep a separate national life from the great American national life around him. Let him become an American citizen, instead of a government ward, and there will be some chance of his holding his property. The Indian Territory must be opened to the farmer and the cattleman.—[Col. L. S. Record.
articles.summary: Clipping (Col. L. S. Record) on a proposed Cherokee convention about wire-fence monopoly, urging the Indian Territory be opened.

articles.text: Reports from all over the country are most flattering for the stockmen. The calf crop while not so large as hoped for, shows an increase over that of last year. The grass everywhere is luxuriant, and during the coming winter the stock on all the ranges will have ample feed. Should the winter be as severe as predicted by would-be weather prophets, the abundance of feed will carry the stock through. It is stated that never within the history of stock raising in this country has the outlook been so hopeful, and we hope all that is expected by owners of herds may be realized.—[Helena Independent.
articles.summary: Clipping (Helena Independent): flattering range reports, luxuriant grass and an increased calf crop.

articles.text: Cattle receipts on the Chicago market were larger during the week than for the week previous. The prices have been generally fair, but not high. The prices of range stock have remained at $4.00@5.00. There was a somewhat better demand for good stock, and the market was more frequently "higher," "brisk" or "steady" than at any previous time during the present season. Some shippers are sanguine that the market will soon assume a better aspect, that prices will advance a trifle, and that the demand for their shipments will be a little more spirited.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.
articles.summary: Clipping (N. W. L. S. Journal) on Chicago cattle receipts and range-stock prices of $4.00@5.00.

articles.text: Pat Ryan, one of the pioneer stockmen of this section, who is located on the Mulberry, a small stream emptying into the Arkansas river, eighteen miles southeast of Dodge, has what may truly be termed a living curiosity, in the shape of a calf that was born about two weeks ago which has not a single hair on its head or body, and but a few scattering ones on its legs. The skin of the young animal seems to be considerably bronzed and hardened. It is fully developed and appears as strong and vigorous as any calf in the herd. It is virtually a curiosity to behold. Mr. Ryan proposes to take the best of care of the young animal and see what it will make.—[Globe Live Stock Journal.
articles.summary: Clipping (Globe Live Stock Journal): Pat Ryan near Dodge has a hairless calf.

articles.text: The New York butchers have endeavored to boycott Chicago beef. Inspector Myers was sent, in consequence of their protests, to Chicago to investigate the condition and circumstances of the beef. He says in his report: "In every instance I found, from the time the bullock is slaughtered until it is ready for shipment, the closest attention is given to cleanly and healthful methods. Scrupulous care was observed in excluding animals where any suspicions of disease existed, and I could not suggest a single improvement. In my opinion the board of health will have to look elsewhere than Chicago to find violations of the law, and I shall so report to that body.—[Col. L. S. Record.
articles.summary: Clipping (Col. L. S. Record): Inspector Myers reports favorably on Chicago beef after a New York butchers' boycott.

articles.text: John A. Blair returned from his northwestern trip last week, after having viewed the beauties of nature from the peaks around the Yellowstone Park and the fair daughters of the northwest from the car windows as he passed villages that have sprung into existence in the past year or so. He is perfectly fascinated with that region as a stock-growing country. The winters are severely cold, of course, but the temperature is so even and the atmosphere so dry and rains so seldom that the stock go through with but little suffering. His company located another ranch of about six miles square adjoining their old ranch, some 35 miles northwest of Glendive. Yearling steers from the States are selling there at $20 to $23, according to class.—[Caldwell (Kan.) Journal.
articles.summary: Clipping (Caldwell Journal): John A. Blair returns from the Northwest; his company located a new ranch some 35 miles northwest of Glendive.

articles.text: The all-important question now for stockmen is how to ship their beef to market. It is not probable that there will be any more buyers in the markets this season, and owners will be compelled to ship. The most economical way to do this is for a number of herd-owners to club together and contract for the transportation. The Northern Pacific railroad company has shown a disposition to be very fair in its arrangement for the shipment of cattle, and we have no doubt that by clubbing together very satisfactory rates may be made. A gentleman representing a herd of 11,000 head, whose range is near Fort McKinney, contracted last week with the Northern Pacific railroad company for 200 cars at $112 per car. The beeves have to be driven 200 miles before shipment. Forty cars have already been side-tracked for the purpose of loading. It would also be well to rent pastures near Chicago and turn the stock on them. Then go into the city and have the cattle brought in at such times as the market is best. It may be easily arranged to ship in from one to three carloads of beeves any day there is demand for them and good prices. This will be found much better than to unload large herds at the yards and take the chances of the market being overstocked.—[Rocky Mountain Husbandman.
articles.summary: Clipping (Rocky Mountain Husbandman) urging herd-owners to club together to ship beef; a Fort McKinney herd contracted 200 Northern Pacific cars at $112 per car.

Patent-inside page: syndicated editorial filler under a Bad Lands Cow Boy heading (Texas growth, Thoreau and bathing, wheat crop, school book question), "News of the Week" wire digest, Foreign Flashes, Dakota News Notes, Republican Campaign Notes, "Demands Cleveland's Withdrawal," and the story "A Fight for Life."

articles.text: Theodore Roosevelt, in a letter to the New York Tribune, declares that Gov. Cleveland's reasons for vetoing the tenure of office bill are "frivolous;" that it is difficult for him to believe "that they were offered in good faith;" and that "it is sheer nonsense to say that the amendment (the Dayton amendment) hurt the bill; on the contrary, it improved it."
articles.summary: Ready-print "Republican Campaign Notes" item: Theodore Roosevelt's letter to the New York Tribune calling Gov. Cleveland's reasons for vetoing the tenure of office bill "frivolous." Transcribed because it names TR; the rest of the page is syndicated filler.

Patent-inside page: cattle-disease interview, agricultural fairs list, miscellany ("At the Right Time," "Some Facts About Peppermint," "A Touching Incident") and patent-medicine ads (Cuticura, Hunt's Remedy, Perry Davis' Pain-Killer, Hostetter's Bitters, Tutt's Pills, St. Jacobs Oil, Parsons' Purgative Pills).

articles.text: The painters will finish painting the warehouse to-day.
articles.summary: Painters to finish painting the warehouse today.

articles.text: Mr. Duncan, of Mandan, was in town a few days during the past week.
articles.summary: Mr. Duncan of Mandan spent a few days in town.

articles.text: C. E. Dow, of the Pioneer furniture store, Mandan, was in town to-day.
articles.summary: C. E. Dow of the Pioneer furniture store, Mandan, was in town.

articles.text: Carpenters are repairing the damage done by the recent storm to the depot.
articles.summary: Carpenters repairing storm damage to the depot.

articles.text: Rev. Father Martin, of Mandan, was here Tuesday, and held mass at the Pyramid Park hotel.
articles.summary: Father Martin of Mandan held mass at the Pyramid Park hotel on Tuesday.

articles.text: J. D. Sears, boot and shoe merchant of Glendive, is in town looking up a location for a branch store.
articles.summary: J. D. Sears of Glendive seeks a location for a branch boot and shoe store.

articles.text: Mr. Miles, a representative of the Armour Bros., was in town this week. He accompanied the Marquis west.
articles.summary: Mr. Miles of Armour Bros. visited and went west with the Marquis.

articles.text: Harry A. Ahl, correspondent of the New York Mercury, came up from Deadwood this week. He is visiting Eaton's ranch.
articles.summary: New York Mercury correspondent Harry A. Ahl came up from Deadwood and is visiting Eaton's ranch.

articles.text: Mr. A. Boyd has suceeded Frank Moore to the management of the Pyramid Park hotel, who is repairing and otherwise improving the house.
articles.summary: A. Boyd succeeds Frank Moore as manager of the Pyramid Park hotel.

articles.text: K. C. Meecher, an English gentleman who has been staying at Lang's ranch for some time on a hunt, went west last night en route to the Canadian Pacific country on a bear hunt.
articles.summary: Englishman K. C. Meecher, a guest at Lang's ranch, left for a bear hunt in Canadian Pacific country.

articles.text: Mr. Grantier, Northern Pacific carpenter foreman, has completed at the warehouse a very neat and commodious office and baggage room, which will be occupied by the Medora Stage and Forwarding company.
articles.summary: N.P. carpenter foreman Grantier finished an office and baggage room at the warehouse for the Medora Stage and Forwarding company.

articles.text: A number of Northern Pacific and St. Paul notables, including Passenger Agent Fee, Vice-President Oakes (possibly), representatives of St. Paul papers and others will visit the Hills by the first coach.—Deadwood Times.
articles.summary: Clipping (Deadwood Times): N.P. and St. Paul notables to ride the first coach to the Black Hills.

articles.text: Marquis de Mores arrived from the east on his special car Monday evening, departing again the following day for Miles City, where he attends the meeting of the Northwestern Live Stock Association. From there he goes to Billings and Helena.
articles.summary: The Marquis de Mores arrived Monday evening and left Tuesday for the Northwestern Live Stock Association meeting at Miles City, then Billings and Helena.

articles.text: Mr. T. J. Kerr, traveling auditor of the Northern Pacific Refrigerator Car company, returned from the west yesterday morning. He reports both the wholesale and retail business of the company's various houses along the line in a flourishing condition.
articles.summary: T. J. Kerr, traveling auditor of the N. P. Refrigerator Car Co., returned from the west and reports business flourishing.

articles.text: Wm. Tinfrock and Sam Tary came down from Helena with Mr. Deffenbach and will be employed by the Medora Stage and Forwarding company. The former as blacksmith and the latter as conductor, head breakman and switchman. Both are men of experience, Sam having manipulated the ribbons for eighteen years.
articles.summary: Wm. Tinfrock (blacksmith) and Sam Tary (driver) came from Helena to work for the Medora Stage and Forwarding company.

articles.text: Mr. Chas. Turner has made a general clean-up around the abattoir this week, and the nauseating oder which prevailed around the establishment has been thoroughly remediated. Next week they will commence slaughtering on a large scale. Mr. Turner is an expert in everything pertaining to the beef trade, and the business hereafter will be under his personal supervision.
articles.summary: Chas. Turner cleaned up the abattoir; large-scale slaughtering to begin next week under his supervision.

articles.text: The lands of the Northern Pacific railroad company will hereafter be sold, in quantities not exceeding 320 acres, to parties who agree to become actual settlers within one year from date of purchase on ten years's time. Terms, one-tenth cash down, and at the end of the first year seven per cent. on balance, one-tenth principal and interest at the end of each succeeding year.
articles.summary: Northern Pacific lands to be sold in tracts up to 320 acres to actual settlers on ten years' time.

articles.text: A herd of buffalo, numbering between two to three hundred, made its appearance seven miles south of here one day last week. Lloyd Roberts and two others who sighted the herd succeeded in killing three of them, and undoubtedly would have slaughtered more had they not run out of ammunition. Wm. Vandriesche purchased one of the heads, which was a very fine one, and shipped it to Mandan for mounting.
articles.summary: A buffalo herd of 200-300 appeared seven miles south of Medora; Lloyd Roberts and two others killed three; Wm. Vandriesche shipped a head to Mandan for mounting.

articles.text: Supt. Deffebach and Mr. Barr arrived Sunday evening from Helena, where they had been to purchase stock for the stage line. They evidently found a good market, as they brought an excellent lot of horses, which were purchased way below eastern prices. The horses arrived here without any very serious accident, except that two were somewhat disabled, but all were more or less bruised by being knocked around in the cars. A few days of feeding grain and grazing will fit them for work.
articles.summary: Supt. Deffebach and Mr. Barr arrived Sunday evening from Helena with horses bought for the stage line.

articles.headline: Belfield Newslets.
articles.text: F. H. Ertel has accepted a position on the Bismarck Journal as business manager and assistant editor.
articles.summary: F. H. Ertel joins the Bismarck Journal as business manager and assistant editor.

articles.text: L. D. Pettit is erecting a fine residence, which will be ready for occupancy in about two weeks. We are pleased to note this fact, as he is one of the live men of our town, and indicates that he will reside here permanently.

articles.headline: Horse Thieves in the Toils.
articles.text: About the first of July three horses were stolen from Robert Milligan, of Sully Springs, and no trace of them could be found until a short time ago when information was received that they were in the hands of an Indian at Standing Rock agency, the Indian having traded for them on the prairie. Sheriff Cuskelly and Milligan started for the agency, and after arriving there and satisfying Agent McLaughlin that the horses belonged to Milligan they were turned over, but not without a vigorous protest from the Indian. A good description of the parties who traded with the Indian was obtained, and they are undoubtedly men who were around here all last spring and well known to all our citizens. The sheriff and Milligan stopped at the camp of "Crow Joe" and learned from him that while Sitting Bull and one of his band were taking a meal at his camp one of the same parties rode up and attempted to steal the old chief's horses, but was discovered and the Indians mounted two of "Crow Joe's" ponies and started in pursuit, overtaking him in a short time when shots were exchanged and the thief captured. After recovering their horses the Indians had no further use for the thief, and instead of taking his scalp, as they should have done, allowed him to go. The sheriff and Milligan arrived here Monday with the horses.—[Dickinson Press.
articles.summary: Clipping (Dickinson Press): horses stolen from Robert Milligan of Sully Springs were recovered at Standing Rock agency; a thief who tried to steal Sitting Bull's horses was caught and released.

articles.headline: NOTICE OF CONTEST.
articles.text:
U. S. Land Office, Bismarck, Dak., July 9, 1884.

Complaint having been entered at this office by John Weber against John Peehn[?] for abandoning his homestead entry No. 153[3?], dated April 9, 1883, upon the SE¼, section [20?], township 140, range 99, in Billings county, Dakota, with a view to the cancellation of said entry; the said parties are hereby summoned to appear at this office on the 21st day of August, 1884, at 10 o'clock A. M., to respond and furnish testimony concerning said alleged abandonment.

J. A. Rea, Register.
O. F. Davis, Att'y for Contestant. 24-5t
articles.summary: Land-office notice of John Weber's contest against a Billings county homestead entry for abandonment, hearing set for August 21, 1884 (standing notice).
